1, The comparison is unfair for the algorithms in Table 1. As described in the paper 'We add squeeze-and-excitation layer to this model at the end of each operator and use mixup during the training of resulted model', both PC-NAS-S and PC-NAS-L used SE module in the architecture and mixup for the training. However, all the comparison algorithms in Table 1 don't use these tricks. According to some published papers, SE module can easily bring 1-2% absolute improvement in ImageNet task. To me, it's unclear whether the performance gain is brought by the tricks (SE + mixup) or the authors' new method.  Thus, more experiments are needed to convince the readers.

2, The comparison is unfair for EA algorithm in Table 3. The population size in EA is set to 5. However, 5 is too small for EA in NAS to work well, e.g., in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.00193.pdf, its population size is 20, in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.00420.pdf, it is set to 50 , in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1812.08934.pdf, it's 96, and in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.01548.pdf. it's either 64 or 256. The number of architectures evaluated during the search is 20*21*900=378000, where 900 is the P value, 21 is the number of mixoperators, and 20 is the number of operators in large search space.  A simple baseline is to use oneshot + random search, where the number of random selected models is 378000. And EA usually performs better than random search. Thus, more fair comparison is needed for Table 3.

content.comment:
We have noticed that properly evaluating the search phase of neural architecture search is of importance. Many existing NAS methods are not better than random architecture selection (suggested by NIPS19's works and other recent works). To justify the effectiveness of a NAS method, model ranking is necessary. 

However, the comparison of model ranking in Figure 2 (b) is not fair. The curve, showing the model ranking of the final stage of architecture search, does not indicate a good evaluation of the proposed search method. It's known that fully training the candidate architectures in the search space leads to better model ranking (see FairNAS and other recent works). In Figure 2 (b), the search space has been narrowed down to an extremely small one. Hence, the candidate architectures in the search space have been fully trained, which results in the good curve shown in Figure 2 (b). A curve showing the model ranking of the early stage of the search with a large search space is desirable.
content.title: Unfair comparison of model rankings

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper builds upon one-shot neural architecture search (NAS), an established technique that consists of the following stages: 1) training a supergraph that can be viewed as a search space (i.e. a one-shot model that includes multiple overlapping candidate architectures), 2) ranking candidate architectures extracted from the trained one-shot model based on their validation accuracy, and 3) training the top candidates from scratch and evaluating them on the test set. The authors point out that the validation set accuracies produced by the one-shot model in step 2) are less predictive of the accuracies produced by stand-alone model training as the number of candidate architectures grows. They name this phenomenon posterior fading. To mitigate this effect, they propose Posterior Convergent NAS (PC-NAS), a method that trains the supergraph in multiple intervals (one interval per mixop/layer). In each interval, a limited pool of candidates (P=5) is selected via a process similar to beam search. The supergraph is trained based on the losses produced by this small number of candidates, thus limiting posterior fading. Experiments are conducted on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection and Market-1501 person re-identification.

A mathematical derivation of the effect of number of architectures in the supergraph on the divergence of  distribution of one-shot estimated parameters as compared to the distribution obtained by training individual models is included. The derivation is a bit sloppy and contains unrealistic assumptions such as that the parameters in different layers/operations are independent. 

The authors conduct experimental comparisons with prior related works using similar search spaces, as well as ablation of the novel components of their approach.

Better performance compared to related work is obtained, but an additional SE layer is used in the current work, which may account for a large part of the gains. If more operators are available in the search space, prior work is clearly outperformed (Table 1).


Ablations of the novel components: layer-wise beam search with pool P for finding top P candidates in a super-graph (Table 3, row 2) and additionally, re-training a shrinking space of models (the full algorithm, Table 3, row 1) , compared to another search method EA (Table 3, row 3) are presented. I don’t know whether EA is a strong search baseline. 
The additional re-training helps 77.1 → 78.1 , but an important question is not answered:
If only beam search without re-training is done, would there be more gains from evaluating more models while using the same computational resources for the search? Since re-training takes 100 additional epochs and training is more expensive than evaluation, additional models (larger P, larger S for Algorithm 1) could have been used.

If the authors  can provide more convincing evidence that the iterative re-training provides a better search complexity / accuracy trade-off compared to established search baselines and the proposed approach without re-training, as well as clean up the writing and improve the derivation to drop the independence assumption, the paper could be accepted.

-------

Some examples of sloppy math:

In Section 3.2 
p_alone(\theta_{m_k}|..) = p_alone(\theta_{m_k}|..). p_alone(\hat{\theta_{m_l}) | ..) 
I believe this should be proportional instead of equal

In section 3.3.
Partial model pool : l-1 selected operators but listing o_1 to .. o_l

There are also many grammatical and language use mistakes.

content.title: Answer to  AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
Q(1):"Assumptions ... parameters in different layers/operations are independent."

Ans(1): The assumption of layer-wise independence is not the case in a plain neural network. However, in this work we refer layer to different choice of computation blocks across the whole supergraph. For a single layer, its parameter $\theta_{l,o}$ is affected by all the remaining layers. The layer-wise independence could be seen as doing a variational inference to the true posterior. The variational distribution $q_{\phi}(\theta)$ is layer-wise independent $q_{\phi}(\theta)=\pi_{l,o}q_{\phi_{l,o}}(\theta_{o,j})$. The assumption is reasonable if the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of previous variational inference could be optimized to sufficiently large. Empirically, we analyse the correlation between one-shot accuracy and stand-alone accuracy with and without our progressive search space shrinking in Figure 2(b). We believe that our analysis here, although based on strong assumption, can be important towards further analysis.    

Q(2):"an additional SE layer is used in the current work, which may account for a large part of the gains"

Ans(2): Thanks for your kind advice on making the comparison more convincing. We apologize for not clarifying the performance boost of our method. The current state-of-the-art results we mainly compare with in this paper are EfficientNet and MixNet. They both use SE layers in their discovered models and the results we list in Table 1 are the accuracies after adding these SE layers. The authors did not list any "no SE" results in their original paper. As suggested by you as well as other reviewers, we add PC-NAS(without SE) versions to the Table 1 of the revised version, which are 76.1% and 77.5% for PC-NAS-S and PC-NAS-L respectively. We compare models separately (with or without SE) and our PC-NAS models achieve new state-of-the-art results in either case. More details on this problem are discussed in our answers to AnonReviewer2.

Q(3): "I don’t know whether EA is a strong search baseline"

Ans(3): Generally speaking, our method could be classified as a sampling based method. And there are two well established sampling based methods: Evolutionary Algorithm and random search. It is widely admitted that EA methods outperform random search consistently. That is why we use it as baseline.

Q(4): "If only beam search without re-training is done, would there be more gains from evaluating more models while using the same computational resources for the search"

Ans(4): We really appreciate your advice on our method. We tried beam search without re-training but with doubled population P or evaluation number S. The accuracies are 77.4% and 77.2% respectively on Imagenet dataset. In comparison, our approach with retraining but the original P and S has accuracy 78.1%. Therefore, enlarging P and S without retraining achieves impressive results, but still not as good as our current version. Without retraining, all estimations are based on the shared weights. Since the Posterior Fading phenomenon, these weights cannot represent the stand-alone accuracy very well. The re-training process brings better model ranking and 0.7%-1% accuracy boost.

content.review: Let me start by saying I am not an expert in architecture search, and putting lowest confidence accordingly.  Nevertheless, I have concerns about this paper.    While the basic idea of progressive search is reasonable,  it is not tightly coupled to the Bayesian argument the authors use to motivate it.  This argument makes some unnatural assumptions (e.g. layers are independent); and the authors do not give any rigorous analysis, either theoretical or empirical,  of how their progressive search method mollifies the posterior fading problem they discuss.  IMO, the whole Bayesian setup makes the motivation unnecessarily complex, and is math for maths sake, rather than for clarification.  The authors do try to show that the final results are better (which isn't the same thing as saying that the method is fixing posterior fading); but I don't think these experiments are convincing.  In particular, the authors seem to use different regularizers than there competitors, and it is not clear where from where the performance gains come.

content.title: Answer to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Q(1): "While the basic idea of progressive search is reasonable, it is not tightly coupled to the Bayesian argument the authors use to motivate it"

Ans(1): 
We sincerely thank you for your valuable advice. We are really sorry for not clarifying the connection between our method and the Bayesian argument. Generally, one-shot methods are widely used in NAS community for its high efficiency. However, there is a long-standing problem in this method: one cannot reliably rank the models based on shared weights. More precisely speaking, the correlation between one-shot accuracy and stand-alone accuracy is low, see Figure 2(b). First, we analysis the problem of weight sharing by formulating it in a bayesian manner. To the best of our knowledge, there is no previous work formulates the weight sharing mechanism. Further more, we show that the KL divergence between one-shot weight parameter distribution and stand-alone weight parameter distribution is the summation of multiple positive valued cross entropy terms. This means that KL-divergence grows with the number of architectures in the search space. In order to reduce the KL-divergence, we propose the progressive search space shrinking.

Q(2):"unnatural assumption - layers are independent"

Ans(2): The assumption of layer-wise independence is not the case in a plain neural network. However, in this work we refer layer to different choice of computation blocks across the whole supergraph. For a single layer, its parameter $\theta_{l,o}$ is affected by all the remaining layers. The layer-wise independence could be seen as doing a variational inference to the true posterior. The variational distribution $q_{\phi}(\theta)$ is layer-wise independent $q_{\phi}(\theta)=\pi_{l,o}q_{\phi_{l,o}}(\theta_{o,j})$. The assumption is reasonable if the evidence lower bound (ELBO) of previous variational inference could be optimized to sufficiently large. Empirically, we analyse the correlation between one-shot accuracy and stand-alone accuracy with and without our progressive search space shrinking in Figure 2(b). We believe that our analysis here, although based on strong assumption, can be important towards further analysis.  

Q(3):"...how their progressive search method modifies the posterior fading problem they discuss "

Ans(3):Thanks for your kind advice that makes the analysis more complete. Theoretically, our method reduces the KL divergence between true parameter distribution and the one-shot parameter distribution over $\theta_{\mathcal{l,o}}$, which alleviates the posterior fading problem. Empirically, we show correlation between one-shot accuracy and stand-alone accuracy with and without our progressive search space shrinking in Figure 2(b). An obvious improvement can be observed. 

Q(4): "...unnecessarily complex, and is math for math sake"

Ans(4):The problem of inaccurate performance of weight sharing is a critical problem in this field, many works have been working on it. However, there is no theoretical formulation of this problem. We try different perspective and find the Bayesian view is the most suitable choice. Bayesian analysis provides insights of this problem and the motivation of the progressive search space shrinking.

Q(5): "...different regularizers"

Ans(5): We apologize for not clarifying the fairness of our comparison experiments. The current state-of-the-art results we mainly compare with in this paper are EfficientNet and MixNet. They both use SE layers in their discovered models and the results we list in Table 1 are the accuracies after adding these SE layers. The authors did not list any "no SE" results in their original paper. As suggested by you as well as other reviewers, we add PC-NAS(without SE) versions to the Table 1 of the revised version, which are 76.1% and 77.5% for PC-NAS-S and PC-NAS-L respectively. We compare models separately (with or without SE) and our PC-NAS models achieve new state-of-the-art results in either case. More details on this problem are discussed in our answers to AnonReviewer2.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper introduces PC-NAS, a new method for architecture search addressing the problem of shared weights in architecture search. 

The authors test the algorithm on ImageNet and show that they are comparable or better than other published methods and also test the model on COCO which is a detection benchmark and show that it holds for the detection and person re-identification tasks.

THe paper is motivated well by identifying a core problem of weight sharing in architecture search and providing a bayesian point of view and a solution for the problem. But, as a few other folks pointed out it is important to do thorough comparisons and it looks like when authors compare the current method to other methods there are other changes to the pipeline that could give boost to the accuracy. So, the claim of achieving state of the art is disputable.

It will be good to decouple the bells and whistles and compare methods on an even footing. If authors can comment on that I still think it is a valuable idea and even if there is no significant delta the work can be a useful contribution.

content.title: Answer to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
Q(1): “Decouple the bells and whistles and compare methods on an even footing”

Ans(1):Thank you for your kind feedback on the fairness of comparison. We apologize for not clarifying the fairness of our comparison experiments. The current state-of-the-art results we mainly compare with in this paper are EfficientNet[1] and MixNet[2]. They both use SE layers[3] in their discovered models and the results we list in Table 1 are the accuracies after adding these SE layers. The authors did not list any "no SE" results in their original paper. As suggested by you as well as other reviewers, we add PC-NAS(without SE) versions to the Table 1 of the revised version, which are 76.1% and 77.5% for PC-NAS-S and PC-NAS-L respectively. We compare models separately (with or without SE) and our PC-NAS models perform consistently better in either case. The results are summarized in the following table.

Model              Latency             Top-1             Top-1(+SE)           
MnasNet             11 ms              74.8%               76.1%
ProxylessNas        8 ms             75.1%                   -
MixNet-S             13 ms                 -                     75.8%
EfficientNet-B0   13 ms                 -                    76.3%
PC-NAS-S             10 ms             76.1%               76.8%
PC-NAS-L             11 ms             77.5%               78.1%

In terms of training script, EfficientNet uses swish[4] and fixed AutoAugment policy[5]. MixNet uses at least swish (complete training details are not quite mentioned in its original paper). These extra bells and whistles used by them have been shown to boost the accuracy a lot[4][5]. Since most of the previous models didn't use these tricks, we didn't use them for more fair comparison. In fact, our PC-NAS models does not benefit from extra bells and whistles when compared with other state-of-the-art models. For reproducibility, the trained model will be released to public upon publication and the setting will be detailed in paper.

[1] Mingxing Tan, Quoc V. Le. EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks, arXiv:1905.11946, 2019

[2] Mingxing Tan, Quoc V. Le. MixConv: Mixed Depthwise Convolutional Kernels, arXiv:1907.09595, 2019

[3] Jie Hu, Li Shen, Samuel Albanie, Gang Sun, Enhua Wu. Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks, arXiv:1709.01507, 2017

[4] Prajit Ramachandran, Barret Zoph, Quoc V. Le. Searching for Activation Functions, arXiv:1710.05941, 2018.

[5] Ekin D. Cubuk, Barret Zoph, Dandelion Mane, Vijay Vasudevan, Quoc V. Le. AutoAugment: Learning Augmentation Policies from Data, arXiv:1805.09501, 2019.
